Sorted soonest first, so the first row is the next one out and next_arrival_minutes answers 'how long have I got?'. Filter by line at a busy interchange to see only the one you take.

get_line_status.description: Check whether named lines are running, and why they are not. Each line comes back with TfL's own wording (Good Service, Minor Delays, Part Suspended), the severity behind it, and the sentence explaining a delay. Branch on has_disruption rather than on the wording, and on all_good to alert only when something is actually wrong.

plan_journey.description: Plan a journey across London the way TfL's own planner does: several options, each with its legs, how long it takes, how many changes it needs and what it costs. Leave the time empty to plan from now, or give one and say whether it is when to leave or when to arrive. Ask for step-free routes, the fewest changes, or particular modes only.

search_stops.description: Find a stop by name and get the code every other action takes. This is how a workflow turns 'Oxford Circus' typed by a person, or read out of an email, into something TfL can answer about. Where a name covers a whole interchange, the stations inside it are listed instead, so every code that comes back works in the arrivals board and the journey planner. Narrow by mode when a name belongs to more than one place, as King's Cross does. TfL returns at most 50 matches.
search_stops.name: search_stops

description: Read London's transport network through TfL's Unified API, the same interface behind TfL's own apps: live line status with the reason for every delay, the arrivals board at any stop, station closures and lift outages, published timetables, the stops and running order of every line, the journey planner with fares and step-free options, road delays, Santander Cycles availability and the London air quality forecast. Lines, stations, modes and roads are dropdowns loaded from TfL, so a step picks a station by name rather than by code. Needs a free TfL API key.
